q: What is the 'fulcrum effect' in laparoscopy?
options: The instrument tip moves opposite to your hand because it pivots at the port
Tissue springs back after being grasped
The camera image is magnified near the port
Instruments feel heavier the deeper they go
explain: Instruments pivot at the body wall, so moving your hand left moves the tip right.
source: Gallagher AG et al., Surg Endosc 1998

q: Which is NOT one of the three criteria of the Critical View of Safety in cholecystectomy?
options: The common bile duct is fully dissected and exposed
The hepatocystic triangle is cleared of fat and fibrous tissue
The lower third of the gallbladder is separated from the liver bed
Only two structures are seen entering the gallbladder
explain: CVS needs a cleared triangle, the lower gallbladder off the liver bed, and exactly two structures (cystic duct and artery). The CBD is not dissected.
source: Strasberg SM, J Am Coll Surg 1995; SAGES Safe Chole

q: Where is McBurney's point?
options: One third of the way from the right ASIS to the umbilicus
Midway between the umbilicus and the pubic symphysis
Two thirds of the way from the umbilicus to the left ASIS
Just below the right costal margin
explain: About 1/3 of the distance from the anterior superior iliac spine to the umbilicus; classic tenderness site in appendicitis.

q: Why is a chest tube passed over the TOP edge of a rib?
options: The intercostal vein, artery and nerve run along the underside of each rib
The lung is further away from the upper border
It is less painful because there is no periosteum
explain: The neurovascular bundle sits in the costal groove on the lower border of each rib.

q: Which borders define the 'safe triangle' for chest drain insertion?
options: Lateral border of pectoralis major, lateral border of latissimus dorsi, and a line at the level of the nipple (5th intercostal space)
Anterior axillary line, costal margin and umbilicus
explain: The apex is just below the axilla; the base is a horizontal line at the nipple / 5th intercostal space.

q: On ultrasound for central line placement, how do you tell the vein from the artery?
options: The vein compresses with gentle probe pressure; the artery stays round and pulsatile
The vein pulses and the artery does not
explain: Veins collapse with light pressure; arteries are non-compressible and pulsatile.
source: AIUM / ACEP ultrasound-guided vascular access guidance

q: What does OSATS stand for?
options: Objective Structured Assessment of Technical Skills
explain: A validated scale rating respect for tissue, time and motion, instrument handling and more.
source: Martin JA et al., Br J Surg 1997

q: In the FLS peg transfer task, what does the trainee do?
options: Lift six rings with one grasper, pass them in mid-air to the other, and place them on pegs on the other side
Cut a circle out of gauze
Place a ligating loop on a foam appendage
explain: Peg transfer trains depth perception and bimanual coordination; cutting and knots are separate FLS tasks.

q: In the common '2 + 1' clipping rule, where do the two clips go when dividing the cystic duct or artery?
options: On the side that stays in the patient
Both on the specimen, one on the patient
explain: Two clips on the retained (patient) side for security, one on the specimen side, then cut between.

q: What is a normal resting heart rate for an adult?
explain: Below 60 is bradycardia and above 100 is tachycardia (athletes can sit lower).

q: What is a normal SpO2 (pulse oximetry) in a healthy adult breathing room air?
explain: Readings below ~92-94% usually warrant attention.

q: What is Betadine (povidone-iodine) used for in surgery?
explain: It kills bacteria on the skin to reduce surgical site infection.
source: WHO Global Guidelines for the Prevention of Surgical Site Infection, 2016

q: What important structure runs in the mesoappendix?
explain: The appendicular artery (from the ileocolic artery) runs in the mesoappendix and must be controlled at appendectomy.

q: The appendicular artery is a branch of which artery?
explain: Ileocolic is a branch of the superior mesenteric artery.

q: What is the usual physiological hand tremor frequency?
explain: Everyone has it; fatigue, caffeine and stress amplify it.

q: Which gas is normally used to inflate the abdomen in laparoscopy?
explain: CO2 is non-flammable and rapidly absorbed, lowering the risk of gas embolism.

q: Why did surgeons lose depth perception when moving from open to laparoscopic surgery?
options: A 2D monitor shows a 3D field, removing stereoscopic cues
explain: Surgeons rely on shadows, texture and instrument cues instead of stereo vision.

q: What does a 'simple interrupted' suture mean?
options: Each stitch is placed and tied separately
One continuous thread runs the whole wound
Stitches are placed under the skin only
Staples are used instead of thread
explain: If one knot fails the others still hold the wound.

q: Lidocaine is most commonly used in laceration repair as a...
explain: It blocks sodium channels in nerves, numbing the area before suturing.

q: In a randomized trial, how did VR-trained residents compare with untrained peers in a real gallbladder removal?
options: About six times fewer errors and 29% faster
explain: A landmark study showing simulation skills transfer to the OR.
source: Seymour NE et al., Ann Surg 2002

q: Most laparoscopic bile duct injuries are caused mainly by...
explain: In 252 cases, most injuries came from misperceiving the common duct as the cystic duct.
source: Way LW et al., Ann Surg 2003

q: What did a NEJM study of bariatric surgeons rated from operative video find?
options: Lower technical skill ratings were linked to more complications and deaths
Skill had no effect on outcomes
Video ratings could not be reproduced
explain: Surgical skill is measurable and directly affects patients.

q: What is 'proficiency-based' training?
options: Practising until you reach an expert benchmark, not for a fixed time
explain: It is the model behind FLS and many simulation curricula.
source: Gallagher AG et al., Ann Surg 2005

q: Passing FLS is required in the US before a general surgery resident can...
options: Sit for American Board of Surgery certification
explain: The American Board of Surgery has required FLS since 2009.
source: American Board of Surgery; SAGES FLS

q: Which organ does a cholecystectomy remove?
explain: 'Chole' = bile, 'cyst' = bladder, '-ectomy' = removal.

q: Surgeons commonly hold a scalpel for a long skin incision using which grip?
explain: The index finger rests on the back of the blade for control along the length of the cut.
source: Standard basic surgical skills courses (e.g. RCS Basic Surgical Skills)
